passage:
When I started freelancing, I thought negotiating meant hiding everything and squeezing the other side. The deal with Arnab's company taught me otherwise.
Arnab ran a small ed-tech firm and wanted illustrations for forty lessons. He offered a rate lower than I'd hoped. I told him the truth: "The rate matters less to me than being paid on time. Last year two clients paid four months late and I had to borrow from my sister."
Then I asked, "What matters most to you?"
He thought. "Speed. We launch in August, and our last illustrator vanished."
So we built the deal around that. I'd deliver in weekly batches; he'd pay each batch within seven days. I took his rate, but with a bonus if we hit August.
We did. It's been two years. Neither of us has ever had to chase the other.
Ishita

qa.q: How many lessons did Arnab want illustrations for?
qa.a: Arnab wanted illustrations for forty lessons.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt telling Arnab about the late payments?
qa.a: Ishita likely felt a little exposed sharing the borrowing, but chose honesty, wanting terms built on the real need to be paid on time rather than a fight over the rate.

qa.q: Which question helped the negotiation most?
qa.a: Asking "What matters most to you?" revealed Arnab's need for speed, which let them design weekly batches, quick payment and a bonus for August.

qa.q: How might Arnab see the deal after two years?
qa.a: Arnab probably trusts Ishita as a reliable collaborator, since the honest terms meant neither of them has ever had to chase the other.

grounding: Ishita negotiates by stating needs truthfully and asking what matters to Arnab, and they build terms that work for both and last.

passage:
Procurement review note. Written by Gautam, purchase head, 22 August.
I sat in on Santosh's first supplier negotiation today, for the packaging order. He is twenty-five and has been with us eight months.
I expected him to push on price, as juniors usually do. Instead he opened by telling the supplier plainly that our real problem was late deliveries in the festival season, not cost. Then he asked, "What makes our orders difficult for you?"
The supplier admitted our last-minute size changes caused most of their delays. Santosh offered to freeze sizes six weeks in advance. In return the supplier agreed to guaranteed festival-season dates and a small discount.
Both sides left relaxed. Nobody was bluffing.
Next steps: I have asked Santosh to write up his approach for the team meeting, and I will propose we adopt the six-week size freeze across all packaging orders.

qa.q: How far ahead did Santosh offer to freeze sizes?
qa.a: Santosh offered to freeze sizes six weeks in advance.

qa.q: What does Gautam's note suggest about Gautam's feelings watching Santosh?
qa.a: Gautam expected a junior to push hard on price, so Gautam seems pleasantly surprised and impressed that Santosh chose honesty and curiosity instead.

qa.q: What made Santosh's negotiation work for both sides?
qa.a: He named the company's real need truthfully, asked what made orders difficult for the supplier, and traded a size freeze for reliable dates.

qa.q: How might the supplier feel about working with this company now?
qa.a: The supplier likely feels heard and less stressed, since the fix for last-minute changes makes their work easier, so they may want to keep the deal.

grounding: A purchase head records a junior buyer who explains needs truthfully, asks what matters to the supplier, and finds terms that work for both.
